summary: Charity Island Light: a brick tower on Big Charity Island in Saginaw Bay, built 1857 and discontinued in 1939 or 1942. Reached by boat.

light.characteristic: White flash every ten seconds from June 1916 (LighthouseFriends).

structures.type: cylindrical brick tower (the archive says conical)
structures.note: 39 ft (12 m) from base to the lantern (archive; LighthouseFriends). Decagonal cast-iron lantern (LighthouseFriends).
Collapsed; removed in 2003 and rebuilt on the old foundation (LighthouseFriends; archive: rebuilt on original foundation).

staffing.note: Keepers until 1916; automated acetylene light from June 1916. Last keeper Joseph N. Singleton (LighthouseFriends).

access.note: Island reached by boat. The keeper's house is privately owned; the tower is owned by The Nature Conservancy. Grounds open, tower closed (LighthouseFriends).

stay.note: The island's owners have a 'Light Keepers House Rental Information' page. Its terms were not read; confirm with the owners.

facts.agency: The Nature Conservancy (tower); private owners (keeper's house)

events.note: Congress appropriated $5,000 for the lighthouse on 18 August 1856 (LighthouseFriends)
Brick tower and keeper's dwelling built on the northwest point, cost $4,819.35
Lens and lamp installed; archive gives 1857 as the year of the original lens
Steamer Oconto grounded on the island in a blizzard, 4 December 1885
Brick oil house with a 360-gallon capacity erected (LighthouseFriends: 1900; the Board's report for the fiscal year ended 30 June 1901 records it)
Keeper McDonald and four men capsized on 6 July 1900; fishermen (LSS letter) or boys and the steamer Sprite (LighthouseFriends) rescued them
Acetylene light installed; light changed to a white flash every ten seconds (June 1916)
Fixed white to flashing white (Bulletin); white flash every ten seconds (LighthouseFriends)
Government sold the island to the Gillingham Fish Company, keeping the lighthouse reservation
Discontinued per the archive and the owners; LighthouseFriends gives 1942
LighthouseFriends: Charity Island Light discontinued when Gravelly Shoal Lighthouse was established
Five Saginaw businessmen acquired the island; GSA top bid of $15,500 for the lighthouse reservation
Bought by private owners; most of the island sold to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and a few acres to the Nature Conservancy
Collapsed keeper's dwelling removed and a new structure built on the old foundation

wrecks.outcome: Caught in a blinding blizzard on Saginaw Bay; her crew mistook the Charity light for the Tawas light and she grounded on the island. Women and children sheltered in the keeper's house; the men in fish huts; the Tawas lifesaving crew helped bring the rest to the mainland.

corrections.why: The archive and LighthouseFriends both date the tower and dwelling to 1857. The 1858 entry comes from Rowlett's directory, which was not read for this research, and no source read supports it.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The archive and LighthouseFriends say the light became an automated acetylene light in June 1916. The Lighthouse Service Bulletin for 1916 says 'oil to electricity'. Two sources against one, so the story follows the registry sources for the illuminant, and flags the Bulletin's wording.
The archive and LighthouseFriends date the tower to 1857, which resolves the record's Rowlett 1858 entry (see corrections).

notes_for_editor: DATES: discontinuance is 1939 (archive; the owners' page) or 1942 (LighthouseFriends, tied to Gravelly Shoal Lighthouse). The Bulletin search (1925-1945) found nothing on Gravelly Shoal or on Charity Island's discontinuance, and the Bulletin volumes after 1939 are not in the corpus. Check the Light List or a Bulletin for 1939-1942 before printing a year. The appropriation of 18 August 1856 is from LighthouseFriends only; the statute and the 1857 Light-House Board record were not read. The 1837 and 1838 reports are quoted through LighthouseFriends, not the originals. The 1900 rescue is in conflict: the Life-Saving Service letter says fishermen rescued the men before the Port Austin and Tawas crews arrived; LighthouseFriends says boys saw them after twenty hours and the steamer Sprite took them off. The story gives both and does not choose. The tower's shape is conical in the archive and cylindrical in LighthouseFriends; the story gives both. The Argus page is OCR'd: the Oconto's passenger numbers are unreadable (LighthouseFriends says 22 passengers and 25 crew), so the story gives no number. The LighthouseFriends account of a cook's death and burial on the island is not in the Argus account and is left out. The LighthouseFriends details about the McDonald family and the wildlife are used with attribution; they come from LighthouseFriends' own account. The owners' page is promotional and is cited only for the 1939 date and the rental page. The owners and the 1992 buyers are not named. The owners' rental page was not read; its terms need checking. The station record's note that LighthouseFriends says 'no access without permission' is not in the LighthouseFriends text read for this research; the story uses LighthouseFriends' 'Grounds open, tower closed'. Confirm current access with the owners and the Nature Conservancy. No photos were added. CHECKED IN PASS 2026-10-28: the story now gives metres in brackets for the eight-foot tower diameter. The 360-gallon oil house is attributed to the Board's report for the fiscal year ended 30 June 1901 (scan p.229), not to 1900. The Alpena Argus account (p.2) is cited for the Oconto's second engineer, the Friday departure, the mistaken light and the ladies and child; the fish huts are described from it. The Tawas lifesaving crew is cited to LighthouseFriends only; the Argus page does not mention it. The Life-Saving Service letter (scan p.199) is headed 'Office of the Light-House Inspector, Eleventh District, Detroit, September 5, 1900'; the story's attribution is correct. The 1916 Bulletin entry is on PDF p.27 (checked by page): 'Charity Island, Mich., fixed white to flashing white, oil to electricity.' Both the archive and LighthouseFriends say acetylene; the owners' page gives 1917 for the automation, which the story does not repeat.
